opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think what's really appealing about the Supermasks in Superposition idea is that it reframes what "learning a task" even means. Instead of updating the weights of a network, you keep the weights fixed and you just learn a binary mask over them, essentially choosing which subnetwork to use for each task. In the original work, that was done on randomly initialized networks, which is already kind of surprising: you can find subnetworks inside a random network that perform well on a given task, and you can store many of those masks for many tasks without them interfering with each other, since the underlying weights never change.

Now, when you think about pretrained models, that picture becomes even more compelling. A large pretrained model presumably already contains a lot of useful structure and features. So the intuition is that, rather than fine-tuning everything and risking overwriting what the model already knows, you could just select the parts of the network that are relevant to a particular task. If a random network already has good subnetworks hidden inside it, a pretrained network should be an even richer starting point for that kind of search.

There are a few practical reasons this is attractive, too. One is catastrophic forgetting: because the base weights stay frozen, learning a new task doesn't degrade performance on old ones. Another is efficiency in terms of storage. A binary mask is very cheap to store compared to a full copy of fine-tuned weights, so you can imagine having one big shared model and a whole library of lightweight task-specific masks that you swap in as needed. And the superposition part of the paper also showed that you can sometimes infer which task you're on by looking at things like the entropy of the outputs under different masks, which hints at a model that can route itself to the right subnetwork.

And then, from a more scientific angle, I just find it interesting as a lens on what's going on inside these networks. If you can recover strong task performance purely by selecting subsets of existing weights, that tells you something about how much capability is already latent in the model and how modular that capability might be. So for me it's both a promising practical tool for adapting pretrained models and a nice way to probe what they've actually learned.

r001.rationale: It says the base weights stay frozen, so learning a new task does not degrade performance on old tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes using a task-specific mask to select relevant parts of a pretrained model, whose existing structure and features provide the starting point for specialization.

r003.rationale: It discusses avoiding overwriting existing knowledge and selecting relevant parts, but does not propose masking connections tied to interfering knowledge to improve downstream performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that excites me about the Supermasks in Superposition work is that it kind of flips how we usually think about what a network is doing when it learns. Normally you think of training as moving the weights around, and the weights are where the knowledge lives. But what Mitchell Wortsman and his collaborators showed, building on the earlier supermask results, is that if you take a fixed, randomly initialized network and just learn a binary mask over it, you can get a surprisingly good subnetwork for each task. The weights never change. All of the task-specific information is in which connections you keep and which you throw away.

For continual learning, that's really attractive, because catastrophic forgetting basically disappears. You're not overwriting anything. Each task gets its own mask, and since the mask is one bit per weight, storing a new one is cheap compared to storing a whole new copy of the model. And then the clever part is the superposition piece: at inference time, if you don't know which task you're on, you can hold a superposition of all the masks and use the network's own output entropy to figure out which one fits, which is a nice, almost gradient-based way of doing task inference.

Now, in the paper they do this on random weights, and the reason I find it promising for pretrained models specifically is that a pretrained network is a much richer substrate than random noise. If a random network already contains good subnetworks for lots of tasks, then a network that's been trained on a huge amount of data should contain much better ones. So I think of masking as a way of asking: what does this model already know how to do, and can I surface it by selecting rather than by fine-tuning? That connects to the work I've done on the lottery ticket hypothesis, where the masks themselves turned out to carry a lot of the signal, and to the supermask idea more broadly.

There's also a practical angle. Fine-tuning a big pretrained model for every downstream task is expensive and you end up with a full copy per task. A mask is a tiny, modular artifact. You can compose them, swap them, store hundreds of them. And because you aren't touching the underlying weights, you preserve whatever general capabilities the pretrained model had, which is exactly the thing fine-tuning tends to erode.

So the short version is: it treats adaptation as a selection problem over existing structure rather than a learning problem that rewrites the model, and pretrained networks are precisely the setting where there's a lot of existing structure worth selecting from. The open question I'm most interested in is how much you lose relative to actual fine-tuning, and whether the gap closes as the base model gets better.

r001.rationale: The response says each task gets its own mask, the underlying weights never change, and catastrophic forgetting basically disappears.

r002.rationale: It describes using masks to surface what a pretrained model already knows by selecting existing structure for a downstream task.

r003.rationale: It says masking can preserve pretrained capabilities, but does not propose masking out connections tied to interfering knowledge to improve downstream performance.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is that you can keep the underlying weights fixed and learn a different mask for each task. The mask selects which connections to use, so adapting the model doesn’t necessarily require changing all of its parameters.

For pretrained models, that suggests a way to reuse one shared set of weights across many tasks, with each task represented by a relatively compact mask. And because learning a new mask doesn’t overwrite the shared weights or the masks for previous tasks, it could help avoid catastrophic forgetting. The question is how well that transfers to large pretrained models—whether selecting the right subnetwork gives you enough flexibility compared with fine-tuning.

r001.rationale: The response says each task gets a mask while the underlying weights stay fixed, and that this could help avoid catastrophic forgetting.

r002.rationale: It describes masks selecting connections and reusing shared weights, but does not clearly explain selecting combinations of features already present in the pretrained model to specialize for a downstream task.

r003.rationale: It does not propose masking out connections associated with interfering knowledge to improve downstream performance.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is that you can adapt a model to different tasks without changing the underlying weights. You learn a task-specific mask that selects a subnetwork, so the same shared weights can support multiple tasks, with each task stored as a relatively lightweight mask.

For pretrained models, that suggests a way to reuse the capabilities already present in the network without keeping a separate fine-tuned copy for every task. And because the weights stay fixed, learning a new mask doesn’t overwrite the weights used by earlier tasks, which is appealing for avoiding catastrophic forgetting. The interesting question is how far that goes—whether a pretrained model already contains subnetworks that are good enough for the downstream tasks we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says the underlying weights stay fixed, so a new task mask does not overwrite weights used by earlier tasks, explicitly connecting this to avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a task-specific mask that selects a subnetwork and reuses capabilities already present in the pretrained network for downstream tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not propose masking out connections associated with interfering knowledge to improve downstream performance.
